tabs.title: Nurses' Notes
tabs.html:
Emergency Department, 1000: A 47-year-old female client reports constant right upper quadrant (RUQ) abdominal pain that began 18 hours ago, about an hour after a fried-food dinner, and now spreads to the right shoulder. Pain 8/10. Nausea with vomiting ×2; has not eaten since. Reports chills overnight and says, 'I feel exhausted and I have no appetite.'

History: obesity (BMI 34), type 2 diabetes (metformin 1,000 mg PO twice daily), hypertension (lisinopril 10 mg PO daily). No known allergies.

Assessment: RUQ tenderness with guarding; the client stops inhaling when the RUQ is palpated. Bowel sounds present. Skin warm and flushed. Alert and oriented ×4.

Abdominal ultrasound: thickened, inflamed gallbladder wall with gallstones, consistent with acute cholecystitis.

tabs.title: Orders
tabs.html:
• NPO
  • Lactated Ringer's IV at 125 mL/hr
  • Morphine 2–4 mg IV every 2 hours PRN severe pain
  • Ondansetron 4 mg IV every 6 hours PRN nausea
  • Ceftriaxone 1 g IV every 24 hours
  • Capillary blood glucose every 6 hours; insulin correction scale
  • Hold metformin
  • Laparoscopic cholecystectomy tomorrow at 0800

questions.stem: Refer to the Nurses' Notes, Vital Signs, and Laboratory Results. The nurse summarizes the client's emergency department data. Which findings require follow-up? Select all that apply.
optionRationales: BP is within normal limits and is a reassuring baseline finding.
Correct. A temperature above 38.5 °C (101.3 °F) is a systemic sign of inflammation.
SpO₂ is normal on room air, so oxygenation is not a current concern.
Correct. Leukocytosis with increased bands (a left shift) shows an acute bacterial inflammatory process with a systemic response.
Creatinine is within normal limits, showing adequate kidney function.
Correct. Inflammation is a physical stress that raises blood glucose, and in a client with type 2 diabetes this level needs follow-up.
questions.rationale: Recognizing cues means separating abnormal, clinically significant data from normal data. Severe RUQ pain, fever, tachycardia (HR 108), and a high WBC with bands show an acute inflammatory process that is producing systemic effects, and the high glucose needs attention in a client with diabetes. Normal BP, SpO₂, mental status, and creatinine are reassuring baseline findings.
questions.takeaway: Fever, tachycardia, and a high WBC with bands mean the inflammation is no longer only local.
questions.hintContent: Recall the systemic signs of inflammation from the nursing assessment and the normal ranges for the labs listed.
questions.hintStrategy: Compare each finding with its normal range and with the client's history. Only abnormal, significant findings require follow-up.
options: BP 136/84 mm Hg
SpO₂ 97% on room air
WBC 15,400/mm³ with 11% bands
Creatinine 0.8 mg/dL
Random glucose 246 mg/dL

questions.stem: Refer to the Nurses' Notes, Vital Signs, and Laboratory Results. Which findings indicate that the gallbladder inflammation is producing a systemic (generalized) inflammatory response? Select all that apply.
optionRationales: Tenderness and guarding are found at the affected organ and reflect local inflammation.
Correct. Fever with chills is a body-wide response to circulating inflammatory mediators.
Stopping inspiration when the RUQ is palpated reflects pain at the inflamed gallbladder, a local finding.
Correct. A high WBC with bands reflects a systemic response by the bone marrow.
Correct. Fatigue and loss of appetite are generalized effects of inflammation.
Pain spreading to the right shoulder is referred pain from the inflamed gallbladder. It reflects the local process, not a body-wide response.
questions.rationale: Local inflammation produces findings at the affected organ: pain, tenderness, guarding, and impaired function. Generalized inflammation produces systemic effects: fever, tachycardia, tachypnea, a rising WBC or bands, fatigue, and loss of appetite. This client has both, so the gallbladder inflammation is producing a generalized response.
questions.takeaway: Findings at the organ are local; fever, high WBC, fatigue, and anorexia are systemic.
questions.hintContent: Recall the difference between localized and generalized inflammation described in the course.
questions.hintStrategy: For each option, ask: would I find this only by examining the RUQ, or does it describe the whole body?
options: RUQ tenderness with guarding
T 38.8 °C (101.8 °F) with chills overnight
The client stops inhaling when the RUQ is palpated
WBC 15,400/mm³ with 11% bands
Fatigue ('I feel exhausted') and loss of appetite
Pain that spreads to the right shoulder

questions.stem: Refer to the Nurses' Notes, Vital Signs, and Laboratory Results. Which statement best describes the client's condition?
questions.rationale: Cholecystitis ('-itis') is inflammation of the gallbladder. Onset over hours after a trigger, with the classic signs at the organ, is acute inflammation, not chronic. Fever, tachycardia, and a high WBC with bands show the response is systemic, while tenderness and guarding are local. Inflammation is a physical stress that raises blood glucose, and this client has diabetes, so the glucose of 246 mg/dL needs follow-up; the other results are normal.
questions.takeaway: Acute cholecystitis with systemic signs; in a client with diabetes, watch the glucose.
questions.hintContent: Recall how the suffix -itis, the time course, and systemic signs help name the problem, and how diabetes affects the response to inflammation.
questions.hintStrategy: Use the time course to decide acute vs. chronic, then decide whether the findings are only local or also systemic.
options: Chronic inflammation of the gallbladder that is limited to the RUQ
Acute inflammation of the gallbladder that is limited to the RUQ
Acute inflammation of the gallbladder with a systemic response
An allergic reaction to fried food with a systemic response
optionRationales: Onset over hours after a trigger is acute, not chronic, and fever and leukocytosis show the process is not limited to the RUQ.
The onset is acute, but fever, tachycardia, and a high WBC with bands show the response has become systemic.
Correct. Cholecystitis is inflammation of the gallbladder. Onset over hours with the classic signs at the organ is acute, and fever, tachycardia, and leukocytosis with bands show a systemic response.
The ultrasound shows an inflamed gallbladder with gallstones, and there are no hives, wheezing, or other signs of an allergic reaction.

questions.stem: Refer to the Nurses' Notes and Orders. The client is admitted to the surgical unit to await cholecystectomy. Which interventions should the nurse include in the preoperative plan of care? Select all that apply.
options: Maintain NPO status and explain the reason to the client
Offer a small, low-fat snack once the nausea improves
Check capillary glucose as prescribed and give correction insulin
Give the prescribed IV morphine for severe pain and reassess
Monitor temperature, heart rate, and respiratory rate for worsening
Give the client's usual morning metformin with a sip of water
optionRationales: Correct: NPO rests the inflamed gallbladder (eating makes it contract) and prepares the client for surgery; explaining why improves cooperation.
Incorrect: the client is NPO; any food stimulates the gallbladder and interferes with surgical preparation.
Correct: inflammation raises glucose in a client with diabetes, and correction insulin is prescribed.
Correct: opioids are used for severe pain; reassessing evaluates the effect.
Correct: rising temperature, HR, or RR would show the systemic response is worsening and must be reported.
Incorrect: metformin is on hold per the orders, and the client is NPO.
questions.rationale: Preoperative care for an inflamed gallbladder rests the organ (NPO), replaces fluids, controls pain, manages glucose in a client with diabetes, and watches for worsening systemic signs. Teaching the reason for each measure is part of the nurse's preoperative role.
questions.takeaway: Before cholecystectomy: NPO, fluids, pain control, glucose checks, and watch the systemic signs.
questions.hintContent: Recall the nurse's preoperative role for a client having surgery for inflammation, and check each option against the Orders.
questions.hintStrategy: Evaluate each option on its own. Eliminate anything that contradicts an order or would stimulate the inflamed organ.

tabs.title: Nurses' Notes
tabs.html: Hospital day 2, 1400: Returned from laparoscopic cholecystectomy at 1100. Four small port-site incisions with dry dressings. Client rates incisional pain 7/10 and is taking shallow breaths, saying, 'It hurts too much to breathe deeply or get up.' Last dose of morphine 2 mg IV at 0930 in the recovery unit. Lungs clear, slightly diminished at the bases. Alert and oriented ×4.

tabs.title: Orders
tabs.html:
• Morphine 2 mg IV every 2 hours PRN severe pain
  • Incentive spirometer 10 times every hour while awake
  • Ambulate in the hallway this evening
  • Clear liquids; advance diet as tolerated
  • Capillary blood glucose every 6 hours; insulin correction scale

questions.stem: Refer to the postoperative Nurses' Notes, Vital Signs, and Orders. Which action should the nurse take first?
options: Coach the client to use the incentive spirometer now
Help the client walk in the hallway right away
Notify the surgeon that the pain is rated 7/10
Administer the prescribed PRN morphine 2 mg IV
optionRationales: Deep breathing is important, but the client cannot do it effectively while pain is severe. Treat the pain first, then coach.
Early walking is ordered for this evening, and severe pain would limit it now. Relieve pain first.
Moderate-to-severe pain a few hours after surgery is expected, the last dose was more than 4 hours ago, and a PRN order is available. There is no new finding to report.
Correct. Pain is limiting deep breathing and movement, and the last dose was given more than 4 hours ago. Relieving it first lets the client use the incentive spirometer and walk.
questions.rationale: Postoperative care after surgery for inflammation includes comfort measures and restoring activity. Opioids are used for severe pain. When pain prevents deep breathing and walking, the nurse gives the prescribed analgesic first and then coaches the incentive spirometer and ambulation once it takes effect. The client's vital signs are improving, and the pain is expected after surgery, so escalation is not needed.
questions.takeaway: Treat the pain that is blocking recovery, then breathe and move.
questions.hintContent: Recall how uncontrolled pain affects deep breathing and mobility after surgery, and when an opioid is indicated.
questions.hintStrategy: All four options may happen. Pick the one that makes the others possible and is within the orders.

tabs.title: Nurses' Notes
tabs.html: Hospital day 3, 0800 (postoperative day 1): Walked in the hallway twice. Pain 3/10 with movement. Tolerating clear liquids without nausea. Port-site incisions clean and dry with edges together; no redness or drainage. While reviewing discharge teaching, the client says, 'Now that my gallbladder is gone, I'll go right back to my fast-food lunches every day.'

questions.stem: Refer to the Nurses' Notes, Vital Signs, and Laboratory Results for postoperative day 1. Which finding is the priority for the nurse to address before discharge?
optionRationales: Temperature and heart rate have returned to normal, showing the systemic response is resolving.
WBC and bands are now within normal limits, showing expected progress after surgery and antibiotics.
Clean, dry incisions with approximated edges show expected healing.
Correct. The client plans to return to a Western-style diet, a modifiable risk factor for inflammation. This teaching need must be addressed before discharge.
questions.rationale: Evaluating outcomes means comparing current data with earlier data and the expected course. The systemic markers and the incisions show the inflammation is resolving after surgery. The client's diet plan shows a teaching need: patient teaching about nutrition is part of the nurse's postoperative role, and avoiding the Western diet is a modifiable risk factor for inflammation.
questions.takeaway: Falling CRP, normal vital signs, and a clean incision = progress; a fast-food plan = more teaching.
questions.hintContent: Recall what a falling CRP means and which dietary patterns promote or reduce inflammation.
questions.hintStrategy: Compare each finding with Day 1 and with normal values. The priority is the one finding that does not show expected progress.
options: Temperature 37.1 °C (98.8 °F) and heart rate 80/min
WBC 9,100/mm³ with bands down to 4%
Port-site incisions clean and dry with edges together
The client's plan for daily fast-food lunches

tabs.title: Nurses' Notes
tabs.html: 1000: A 68-year-old female client with rheumatoid arthritis is admitted with weakness and dizziness when standing. For 4 months she has taken naproxen 500 mg PO twice daily and adds over-the-counter ibuprofen 'when my joints are bad.' Reports 'black, sticky stools' for 2 days and a burning pain in the upper abdomen. Skin pale and cool. Alert and oriented ×4.

questions.stem: Refer to the Nurses' Notes, Vital Signs, and Laboratory Results. Which actions should the nurse take at this time? Select all that apply.
optionRationales: Correct. Black, sticky stools, upper abdominal pain, and a falling hemoglobin suggest an NSAID-induced upper GI bleed, so the drugs are held and the provider notified.
Taking an NSAID with food or milk may reduce stomach upset, but it does not stop an active bleed, and continuing the drug is unsafe.
Correct. The BP drop and dizziness on standing show significant blood loss and a high risk for falls.
Aspirin also blocks prostaglandins that protect the stomach lining and impairs clotting, so it would worsen bleeding.
Correct. Hemoglobin, BP, and HR show whether bleeding continues and whether the client is responding to treatment.
Diet changes address long-term iron stores and bowel habits; they do not treat acute bleeding.
questions.rationale: Prostaglandins cause pain, fever, and swelling but also protect the stomach lining. NSAIDs block them, so long-term use, especially of two NSAIDs together, can cause ulcers and GI bleeding. Melena, upper abdominal pain, a falling hemoglobin, and a BP drop with tachycardia on standing show significant blood loss. The nurse holds the NSAIDs, notifies the provider, protects the client from falls, and monitors hemoglobin, BP, and HR.
questions.takeaway: NSAIDs + black stools + dizziness = GI bleed: hold, notify, prevent falls, trend Hgb and vital signs.
questions.hintContent: Recall why NSAIDs damage the stomach lining and what black, sticky stools and a BP drop on standing mean.
questions.hintStrategy: Decide what condition the findings point to, then choose only actions that treat or monitor that condition now. Eliminate prevention teaching and anything that continues the cause.
options: Hold the NSAIDs and notify the provider
Teach the client to take the naproxen with milk
Use fall precautions and help the client get up slowly
Replace the naproxen with aspirin for the joint pain
Monitor hemoglobin, blood pressure, and heart rate
Encourage iron-rich foods and more dietary fiber

tabs.title: Nurses' Notes
tabs.html: 1030: An 84-year-old client is admitted from a long-term care facility. The client's daughter says the client has been 'not herself' since yesterday: more confused, refused breakfast, and slid to the floor while getting up (no injury). Baseline: oriented to person and place, walks with a walker. Now oriented to person only and picking at the bed linens. Weak, moist cough. Crackles in the right lower lobe. No urinary symptoms reported. Medications: donepezil 10 mg daily, lisinopril 10 mg daily.

questions.stem: Refer to the Nurses' Notes, Vital Signs, and Laboratory Results. Which action should the nurse take first?
optionRationales: Cultures should be obtained before antibiotics are started, but correcting the low oxygen saturation comes first.
Correct. An SpO₂ of 89% with RR 26 is a breathing problem. By the ABCs, oxygenation is the priority, and it may also improve the new confusion.
Comparing mental status with baseline is important for evaluating progress, but it does not treat the low oxygen level.
The urinalysis is negative for leukocyte esterase and nitrite, and the findings point to pneumonia, not a urinary infection.
questions.rationale: Older adults often present with infection atypically: a small rise from their own baseline temperature, new confusion, falls, and loss of appetite rather than a high fever. This client's cough, crackles, tachypnea, low SpO₂, and high WBC with bands point to pneumonia with a systemic inflammatory response. Using the ABCs, the nurse corrects the low oxygen level first, then obtains cultures before the first antibiotic dose, avoids restraints and sedating drugs, and uses mental status and respiratory status to judge progress.
questions.takeaway: In an older adult, new confusion plus a small temperature rise from baseline can be serious infection.
questions.hintContent: Recall how older adults present with infection and why the client's own baseline matters.
questions.hintStrategy: Identify the condition by comparing the data with the client's own baseline, then apply the ABCs to choose the first action.
options: Obtain blood and sputum cultures before the first antibiotic dose
Apply oxygen as prescribed to keep SpO₂ at or above 92%
Compare the client's orientation with the facility baseline
Collect a urine specimen for culture to check for infection

questions.clientNeed: Physiological Integrity: Reduction of Risk Potential
questions.stem: A 64-year-old client's lower-leg wound was left open to heal by secondary intention after an abscess was drained 12 days ago. Which wound assessment findings indicate the wound is NOT progressing through the reparative phase as expected? Select all that apply.
optionRationales: Beefy red, moist, granular tissue is healthy granulation tissue, an expected finding.
Correct. Pale, gray, friable tissue indicates poor blood supply or infection rather than healthy granulation.
Correct. Thick, tan-green (purulent) drainage suggests infection. Drainage should decrease and become serous as the wound heals.
Correct. A foul odor that persists after cleansing suggests infection.
A shrinking wound shows contraction, an expected part of repair.
Correct. Pain should lessen as the wound heals. Rising pain suggests infection or impaired healing.
questions.rationale: In the reparative phase, healthy granulation tissue is beefy red and moist, drainage decreases and becomes serous, pain lessens, and the wound contracts. Pale or gray tissue, purulent drainage, foul odor, and increasing pain indicate infection or impaired healing and should be reported. An infected wound can still have a normal temperature, so local findings matter.
questions.takeaway: Beefy red is good; gray tissue, pus, odor, and rising pain are not.
questions.hintContent: Picture healthy granulation tissue and the expected trend of drainage and pain as repair progresses.
questions.hintStrategy: For each finding, ask whether it moves toward healing or away from it. Do not skip a finding just because other findings look good.
options: Most of the wound bed is beefy red, moist, and granular
An area of pale, gray, friable tissue at the lower edge
Moderate thick, tan-green drainage on the dressing
A foul odor that persists after cleansing
Wound length decreased from 5.2 cm to 4.1 cm over 1 week
Pain rising from 2/10 to 7/10 over the past 24 hours

questions.ref: Module 10 · Inflammation · Lifespan Considerations – Children & Adolescents
questions.stem: The nurse is caring for an 18-month-old child admitted with pneumonia who has had vomiting and poor oral intake for 2 days. Which finding requires the nurse's immediate follow-up?
optionRationales: Fever needs treatment and increases fluid loss, but it does not show that perfusion is already compromised.
A respiratory rate of 36/min is within the expected range for a toddler.
This BP is within the expected range for a toddler. Children often keep a normal BP until late in shock.
Correct. Lethargy and difficulty arousing show poor perfusion of the brain from fluid loss and require immediate intervention.
questions.rationale: Young children have a smaller total fluid volume and immature kidneys that control fluid balance poorly, so fever, vomiting, and poor intake quickly cause significant fluid loss. Lethargy, delayed capillary refill, and absent urine output show poor perfusion of the brain, skin, and kidneys and need immediate intervention. Do not wait for vital-sign changes to act.
questions.takeaway: In a child, check mental status, capillary refill, and wet diapers.
questions.hintContent: Recall why fluid losses are more significant in young children and which findings reflect perfusion of the brain, skin, and kidneys.
questions.hintStrategy: Children can keep a normal BP until late. Look for the finding that shows an organ is already underperfused.
options: Temperature of 38.9 °C (102.0 °F)
Respiratory rate of 36/min
Blood pressure of 92/58 mm Hg
Lethargy and difficulty arousing

questions.ref: Module 10 · Inflammation · Normal Presentation of Inflammation (Causes)
questions.stem: A client has painful, red, warm skin on both shoulders after a day at the beach without sunscreen. T is 37.2 °C (99.0 °F), and there are no open areas. The client asks, 'If there are no germs, why is my skin inflamed?' Which response by the nurse is best?
options: Bacteria on your skin multiplied in the heat and caused the redness.
UV radiation injured the skin, and inflammation follows any injury.
Your immune system has started attacking your own skin cells.
The redness means an infection is starting and needs antibiotics.
optionRationales: Incorrect: the cause here is a physical agent (radiation), not microorganisms.
Correct: inflammation is a nonspecific response to harm. Physical agents such as radiation, heat, and trauma trigger it just as microorganisms do.
Incorrect: this describes autoimmune disease, not a sunburn.
Incorrect: inflammation is not the same as infection; the classic signs here come from the response to radiation injury.
questions.rationale: Inflammation is triggered by injury, infection, or harmful agents. Its causes include microorganisms, chemical agents (internal acids, external poisons), and physical agents (trauma, heat or cold, radiation). A sunburn is inflammation from radiation, so it shows redness, heat, swelling, and pain without any infection.
questions.takeaway: Inflammation is not infection: physical agents such as UV radiation trigger it too.
questions.hintContent: Recall the three categories of causes of inflammation listed in the course.
questions.hintStrategy: Identify what actually harmed the tissue, then choose the response that names that cause accurately.

questions.clientNeed: Physiological Integrity: Basic Care and Comfort
questions.stem: A client with a sprained right wrist has had a cloth-wrapped cold pack applied for 20 minutes every 2–3 hours and the wrist elevated for 24 hours. Which finding best indicates these measures are achieving the intended effect?
options: The skin over the wrist remains pale and cool 1 hour after the pack is removed
The client reports numbness in the fingers while the cold pack is in place
Bruising over the wrist has spread toward the forearm
Wrist circumference has decreased from 18.5 cm to 17.6 cm
optionRationales: Incorrect: persistent pallor and coolness after removal suggest excessive vasoconstriction or cold injury.
Incorrect: numbness during application signals possible nerve or tissue injury; the pack should be removed.
Incorrect: spreading bruising is gravity-dependent movement of blood, not a sign that cold is reducing swelling.
Correct: cold causes vasoconstriction and reduces capillary leak, and elevation promotes venous and lymphatic return; less swelling is the goal.
questions.rationale: Cold and elevation in the first 24–48 hours limit the vascular phase of inflammation: vasoconstriction reduces blood flow and exudate, and elevation lowers hydrostatic pressure. A measurable decrease in swelling (and pain) shows the intervention is working. Numbness or persistent pallor indicate harm.
questions.takeaway: Measure swelling to evaluate cold and elevation; numbness means stop.
questions.hintContent: Recall what cold and elevation do to blood flow and capillary leakage at an injured site.
questions.hintStrategy: The question asks for evidence the intervention is working. Eliminate findings that show harm or have nothing to do with swelling.

questions.clientNeed: Physiological Integrity: Reduction of Risk Potential
questions.stem: A client reports a painful, swollen left knee after kneeling on a hard floor for several hours. Which technique should the nurse use to determine whether the knee has increased warmth?
options: Compare both knees using the back of the hand
Palpate the left knee firmly with the fingertips
Measure the knee's skin with a tympanic thermometer
Ask the client whether the knee feels warm
optionRationales: Correct: the dorsal surface of the hand is most sensitive to temperature, and comparing with the unaffected knee shows a relative difference.
Incorrect: fingertips are best for fine discrimination, not temperature, and firm pressure causes unnecessary pain.
Incorrect: a tympanic thermometer measures core temperature through the ear canal and is not designed for skin.
Incorrect: the client's perception is subjective; the nurse needs an objective assessment.
questions.rationale: Heat (calor) results from increased blood flow to an inflamed site. The nurse assesses it with the back of the hand, which is most sensitive to temperature, and compares it with the same area on the opposite side, because 'warm' is only meaningful relative to the client's normal.
questions.takeaway: Check warmth with the back of the hand and compare with the other side.
questions.hintContent: Recall which part of the hand is most sensitive to temperature and why bilateral comparison matters.
questions.hintStrategy: Judge each technique for accuracy and objectivity. A useful assessment produces a finding you can interpret against a reference point.

questions.stem: A client who had a myocardial infarction 5 days ago asks, 'Once the inflammation settles down, will my heart muscle grow back?' Which response by the nurse is accurate?
options: Yes, heart muscle fully regenerates within 6 to 8 weeks with rest.
New muscle cells from your bone marrow will replace the damaged area.
The damaged area heals as scar tissue that does not pump.
It will regenerate if you take an anti-inflammatory medicine daily.
optionRationales: Incorrect: cardiac muscle has very limited ability to regenerate.
Incorrect: bone marrow cells do not replace infarcted myocardium in clinical practice.
Correct: tissues with limited regeneration, such as cardiac muscle, heal by scar (cicatrix), which is firm but cannot contract like muscle.
Incorrect: anti-inflammatory drugs do not cause regeneration, and NSAIDs are generally avoided after MI.
questions.rationale: In the reparative phase, tissue is either regenerated or replaced by scar. Skin, GI and respiratory mucosa, bone, and marrow regenerate readily. Cardiac muscle, CNS neurons, and elastic tissue have limited or no regeneration and heal by scar, which cannot contract like cardiac muscle. This explains why cardiac rehabilitation focuses on strengthening the remaining muscle.
questions.takeaway: Heart muscle heals by scar, not regeneration.
questions.hintContent: Recall which tissues regenerate quickly and which heal by scar formation.
questions.hintStrategy: Choose the answer that is both accurate and honest; avoid options that offer false reassurance.

questions.clientNeed: Physiological Integrity: Basic Care and Comfort
questions.stem: A client is recovering from drainage of a thigh abscess, and the wound is now filling with granulation tissue. The client asks for a between-meal snack. Which snack should the nurse recommend to best support this phase of healing?
options: Greek yogurt with sliced strawberries
A bowl of buttered white rice with gravy
Saltine crackers with a diet soda
A glass of apple juice and a rice cake
optionRationales: Correct: yogurt provides protein, and strawberries provide vitamin C; both are needed for collagen synthesis.
Incorrect: this provides calories but little protein or vitamin C.
Incorrect: this provides little protein, vitamin C, or calories.
Incorrect: this is mostly simple carbohydrate, with little protein.
questions.rationale: The reparative phase requires collagen synthesis, which depends on protein (amino acids) and vitamin C. Adequate calories, fluids, and zinc also support healing. A snack combining protein and vitamin C best supports granulation tissue formation.
questions.takeaway: Repair runs on protein and vitamin C.
questions.hintContent: Recall which nutrients are needed to build collagen during repair.
questions.hintStrategy: Identify the nutrients each snack provides, then match them to what the healing wound needs.

questions.clientNeed: Physiological Integrity: Basic Care and Comfort
questions.stem: A client with pneumonia has T 38.9 °C (102.0 °F) and HR 104/min, is sweating heavily, and has taken only 300 mL of oral fluid today. Acetaminophen was given 30 minutes ago. Which nursing action is the priority?
options: Restrict oral fluids to 1 L per day to avoid fluid overload
Add heavy blankets so the client can sweat out the fever
Encourage oral fluids and change damp gown and linens
Place ice packs in the axillae and groin until shivering starts
optionRationales: Incorrect: fever and sweating increase fluid loss. Restricting fluids would worsen the deficit.
Incorrect: heavy blankets trap heat and raise the temperature further.
Correct: adequate fluids replace losses from fever and sweating and support healing, and dry linens and gown are a comfort measure.
Incorrect: ice packs to the point of shivering cause discomfort and increase heat production.
questions.rationale: A temperature above 38.5 °C (101.3 °F) with a HR above 90 is a systemic sign of inflammation that the nurse monitors and reports. Independent interventions for a febrile client include adequate fluids and hydration to support healing, comfort measures such as dry linens and positioning, and rechecking the temperature after the antipyretic.
questions.takeaway: Fever: push fluids, keep the client dry and comfortable, and recheck.
questions.hintContent: Recall the independent interventions that promote healing and comfort during inflammation, including hydration.
questions.hintStrategy: Consider what fever and heavy sweating do to fluid balance, then eliminate options that would worsen fluid loss or discomfort.

questions.ref: Module 10 · Inflammation · Lifespan Considerations – Pregnant Women
questions.clientNeed: Physiological Integrity: Reduction of Risk Potential
questions.stem: A client at 32 weeks' gestation has a BP of 152/98 mm Hg and 2+ proteinuria and is being monitored for preeclampsia, an inflammation-mediated disorder of the blood vessel lining. Which finding should the nurse report to the provider immediately?
options: Mild swelling of both ankles that improves after a night's rest
Severe headache with spots in the vision despite acetaminophen
Needing to urinate more often than before the pregnancy began
A dull lower back ache after standing at work for several hours
optionRationales: Incorrect: dependent ankle edema that resolves with rest is common in the third trimester and is not a severe feature.
Correct: a severe, persistent headache and visual disturbances are severe features of preeclampsia that signal cerebral vasospasm and edema and a risk of eclamptic seizures.
Incorrect: urinary frequency is common in late pregnancy as the uterus presses on the bladder.
Incorrect: low back ache is a common discomfort of pregnancy from postural changes.
questions.rationale: Pregnancy dampens the immune system and alters the inflammatory response. Preeclampsia is an inflammation-mediated hypertensive disorder: inflammation of the blood vessel lining causes vasospasm, high BP, and capillary leak. A new, severe headache and visual changes show the brain is affected and require immediate provider notification because of the risk of seizures and stroke.
questions.takeaway: Preeclampsia plus headache or visual changes = severe feature; report now.
questions.hintContent: Recall how endothelial inflammation in preeclampsia affects the brain and other organs, and which discomforts are common in late pregnancy.
questions.hintStrategy: Separate the common discomforts of the third trimester from findings that suggest a target organ is being affected.

questions.clientNeed: Safe and Effective Care Environment: Management of Care
questions.stem: The RN is caring for an 88-year-old client admitted with pneumonia. The client's baseline temperature is 36.1 °C (97.0 °F). Which instruction is most important for the RN to give the unlicensed assistive personnel (UAP)?
options: Report any new confusion or change in behavior right away
Report the temperature only if it rises above 39 °C (102.2 °F)
Keep the client in bed to conserve energy without offering to walk
Limit the client's fluids to 1 L per day to prevent overload
optionRationales: Correct: a change in mental status is often the earliest sign of worsening infection or hypoxemia in an older adult; the UAP can observe it, and the RN assesses it.
Incorrect: older adults may never reach a high fever; a rise of more than 1.1 °C (2 °F) above baseline is significant.
Incorrect: prolonged bedrest increases the risks of deconditioning, atelectasis, and delirium.
Incorrect: fluid restriction is not indicated and increases the risk of dehydration and thick secretions.
questions.rationale: Older adults have blunted fever responses and often present with atypical signs such as confusion, falls, or loss of appetite. The RN delegates data collection within the UAP's scope and gives clear parameters for reporting. A new change in behavior is a priority finding to report immediately. A high temperature threshold would miss significant fever in this client.
questions.takeaway: In older adults, new confusion may be the first sign of infection; tell the UAP to report it.
questions.hintContent: Recall how infection often presents in older adults and how fever is defined relative to baseline.
questions.hintStrategy: Delegation items need clear, safe reporting parameters. Eliminate options that would delay recognition of a problem or cause harm.

questions.ref: Module 10 · Inflammation · What Inflammation Is (and Isn't)
questions.stem: The nurse is reviewing the admitting diagnoses of clients in an urgent care clinic. Which clients have inflammation that is NOT caused by a microorganism? Select all that apply.
options: A client with sunburn after a day at the beach
A client with strep throat and a positive rapid antigen test
A client with a chemical burn from a drain cleaner
A client with an ankle sprain from a fall
A client with a urinary tract infection from E. coli
A client with contact dermatitis from poison ivy
optionRationales: Correct: sunburn is inflammation from a physical agent (ultraviolet radiation).
Incorrect: strep throat is inflammation caused by a bacterium.
Correct: a chemical agent (an external caustic) caused the tissue injury.
Correct: a sprain is inflammation from a physical agent (trauma).
Incorrect: a UTI is inflammation caused by a bacterium.
Correct: poison ivy dermatitis is an allergic reaction to plant oil (overactive mediators), not an infection.
questions.rationale: Inflammation is a nonspecific response to harm. It is triggered by microorganisms, but also by chemical agents and physical agents, and overactive mediators cause allergic reactions. Recognizing noninfectious inflammation prevents unnecessary antibiotic use and focuses care on the actual trigger.
questions.takeaway: Microorganisms are only one of the triggers of inflammation.
questions.hintContent: Recall the categories of inflammatory triggers: microorganisms, chemical agents, and physical agents.
questions.hintStrategy: Evaluate each client separately. Ask: what exactly caused the tissue harm here?

questions.clientNeed: Physiological Integrity: Basic Care and Comfort
questions.stem: A client sprained the right wrist in a fall 2 hours ago. The wrist is red, warm, and swollen, and there is no wound. Which interventions should the nurse include in the plan of care? Select all that apply.
options: Elevate the wrist above the level of the heart
Apply a cold pack wrapped in a thin towel for 15–20 minutes
Apply a heating pad on high while the client sleeps
Massage the wrist firmly to move the swelling
Wrap the wrist tightly with an elastic bandage overnight
Check capillary refill and sensation in the fingers
optionRationales: Correct: elevation lowers hydrostatic pressure and promotes venous and lymphatic return.
Correct: early cold causes vasoconstriction, which reduces swelling and pain; a barrier protects the skin.
Incorrect: heat increases blood flow and swelling in acute inflammation, and a heating pad on high during sleep risks burns.
Incorrect: firm massage of acutely inflamed tissue increases pain and tissue injury.
Incorrect: a tight wrap left on overnight can impair circulation as swelling changes.
Correct: swelling can compress vessels and nerves, so distal neurovascular checks are essential.
questions.rationale: In acute inflammation, the goals are to limit the vascular response and protect function: rest, cold, and elevation reduce swelling and pain, and neurovascular checks detect compression. Heat is used later, after the acute phase, to promote circulation and comfort.
questions.takeaway: Acute inflammation: rest, cold, elevate, and check what is distal.
questions.hintContent: Recall how cold, heat, and elevation affect blood flow and fluid movement in the acute phase.
questions.hintStrategy: Treat each option as true or false for the acute phase specifically.

questions.clientNeed: Physiological Integrity: Reduction of Risk Potential
questions.stem: The nurse is assessing wound drainage for several clients on postoperative day 3. Which findings should the nurse report to the provider? Select all that apply.
options: A small amount of thin, pale pink drainage on the dressing, less than on day 1
Thick, yellow-green incisional drainage with a foul odor
A sudden increase in bright red drainage saturating the dressing
Scant serous drainage at the edge of the dressing
Cloudy, tan drainage with redness spreading beyond the incision
A dry incision with approximated edges and a firm pink ridge
optionRationales: Do not report: decreasing, paler serosanguineous drainage is the expected trend.
Report: purulent, malodorous drainage indicates wound infection.
Report: a sudden increase in bright red drainage suggests active bleeding.
Do not report: a small amount of serous drainage is expected early in healing.
Report: cloudy drainage with spreading erythema indicates infection spreading into surrounding tissue.
Do not report: a healing ridge under an approximated incision is a normal sign of collagen deposition.
questions.rationale: The type and trend of exudate show how a wound is healing. Serous and serosanguineous drainage that decreases and lightens is expected. Purulent or cloudy drainage, a foul odor, spreading redness, or a sudden increase in bright red drainage are deviations that require provider notification.
questions.takeaway: Report drainage that turns purulent, spreads, or suddenly becomes bright red.
questions.hintContent: Recall the types of exudate and the expected trend in the first days after surgery.
questions.hintStrategy: Look at both the type of drainage and whether it is getting better or worse over time.

questions.ref: Module 10 · Inflammation · Acute vs. Chronic Inflammation
questions.stem: A 34-year-old client has had Crohn's disease for 8 years. Which findings reflect the effects of long-standing chronic inflammation? Select all that apply.
options: Fatigue that persists despite adequate sleep
Loss of appetite that has lasted for months
Symptoms that have persisted and flared over many years
Unintentional weight loss of 5 kg (11 lb) over 6 months
Sudden fever of 40 °C (104 °F) with rigors starting today
Complete resolution of symptoms within 3 days
optionRationales: Correct: persistent fatigue is a common systemic effect of chronic inflammation.
Correct: long-standing appetite loss is a systemic effect of chronic inflammation.
Correct: chronic inflammation lasts months to years.
Correct: chronic inflammation and poor absorption cause weight loss.
Incorrect: an abrupt high fever with rigors suggests a new acute process that needs urgent evaluation.
Incorrect: rapid, complete resolution is characteristic of acute, not chronic, inflammation.
questions.rationale: Chronic inflammation lasts months to years and causes ongoing tissue damage. Its systemic effects include fatigue, loss of appetite, and weight loss. A sudden high fever with rigors suggests a new acute process, and rapid, complete resolution is typical of acute inflammation.
questions.takeaway: Chronic inflammation: years of symptoms with fatigue, appetite loss, and weight loss.
questions.hintContent: Recall the duration and systemic effects of chronic versus acute inflammation.
questions.hintStrategy: For each option, ask whether it develops slowly over time or appears suddenly.

questions.stem: A 5-year-old is admitted with a deep-tissue infection of the thigh that requires IV antibiotics and imaging. Which interventions should the nurse include in the plan of care? Select all that apply.
options: Calculate each medication dose using the child's weight in kilograms
Request a child life specialist to prepare the child for procedures through play
Offer aspirin for fever and discomfort
Monitor urine output and the number of voids
Choose invasive imaging even when a noninvasive option would work
optionRationales: Correct: pediatric doses are weight based to prevent under- or overdosing.
Correct: play and child life preparation reduce fear and improve cooperation with procedures.
Incorrect: aspirin is avoided in children because of the risk of Reye syndrome.
Correct: children have small fluid reserves, and urine output is a sensitive indicator of perfusion.
Incorrect: noninvasive imaging is preferred for children whenever possible.
questions.rationale: Children with inflammatory conditions need age-appropriate care: weight-based dosing, preparation through play and child life support, close fluid monitoring because fluid losses are more significant, noninvasive imaging when possible, and avoidance of aspirin.
questions.takeaway: Children: dose by weight, prepare through play, watch output, prefer noninvasive imaging, skip aspirin.
questions.hintContent: Recall the care considerations for children: dosing, preparation, fluid balance, imaging, and drug safety.
questions.hintStrategy: Judge each option for safety specifically in a 5-year-old.

questions.clientNeed: Physiological Integrity: Reduction of Risk Potential
questions.stem: An 83-year-old client is on postoperative day 3 after hip fracture repair. The client's baseline temperature is 36.2 °C (97.2 °F). Which findings could indicate a developing infection? Select all that apply.
options: New inattention and disorientation to time
Eating 30% of meals, down from 80% yesterday
Incisional pain of 3/10 with movement
Oriented to person, place, and time, as at admission
Decreasing serosanguineous drainage on the dressing
optionRationales: Correct: new delirium is a common atypical presentation of infection in older adults.
Correct: this is 1.2 °C above baseline; a rise of more than 1.1 °C (2 °F) over baseline counts as fever in older adults.
Correct: a sudden decline in appetite is a common nonspecific sign of infection in older adults.
Incorrect: mild pain with movement is expected on postoperative day 3.
Incorrect: unchanged orientation is reassuring.
Incorrect: decreasing serosanguineous drainage is the expected trend.
questions.rationale: Older adults have diminished inflammatory responses and lower baseline temperatures, so infection often presents with subtle findings: new confusion, a small temperature rise from baseline, falls, and reduced appetite. The nurse compares findings with the client's own baseline and reports changes early.
questions.takeaway: Compare an older adult with their own baseline; small changes can be big.
questions.hintContent: Recall how fever is defined in older adults and the atypical signs of infection in this age group.
questions.hintStrategy: Do not judge the temperature against the textbook normal; compare it with the baseline in the stem.

questions.ref: Module 10 · Inflammation · Alterations & Manifestations (Localized vs. Generalized)
questions.stem: A client is admitted with acute pancreatitis. Which findings indicate a systemic (generalized) inflammatory response rather than only local inflammation? Select all that apply.
options: Epigastric tenderness to palpation
Epigastric pain that worsens after eating
WBC 15,200/mm³
Fatigue and loss of appetite
Guarding of the upper abdomen
optionRationales: Local: tenderness is pain at the inflamed organ.
Systemic: a temperature above 38.5 °C shows mediators are acting on the whole body.
Local: pain arising from the inflamed pancreas is a finding at the site.
Systemic: a WBC above 12,000/mm³ reflects the bone marrow response to circulating mediators.
Systemic: fatigue and appetite loss are whole-body effects of inflammation.
Local: guarding reflects pain and impaired function at the site.
questions.rationale: Local inflammation produces findings at the affected organ, such as tenderness, pain, and guarding. When mediators enter the circulation, systemic effects appear: fever, tachycardia, tachypnea, a rising WBC, fatigue, and loss of appetite. Systemic signs help the nurse recognize a more serious or spreading process.
questions.takeaway: Local signs are at the organ; systemic signs are fever, malaise, and leukocytosis.
questions.hintContent: Recall which effects of inflammation are produced at the site and which are produced by circulating cytokines.
questions.hintStrategy: Ask whether each finding could be detected only by examining the abdomen.

questions.clientNeed: Physiological Integrity: Basic Care and Comfort
questions.stem: The nurse is preparing to apply a cold pack to a client's ankle, which was sprained 2 hours ago. Which action should the nurse take first?
options: Wrap the cold pack in a thin cloth barrier
Elevate the ankle on two pillows above the level of the heart
Assess skin integrity, sensation, and circulation
Apply the pack for 15–20 minutes at a time
questions.rationale: Baseline assessment comes first so the nurse can detect injury and identify contraindications such as impaired sensation or circulation. A barrier prevents cold injury, and limiting application to 15–20 minutes prevents rebound vasodilation and tissue damage. The skin is inspected after removal, and the response is documented.
questions.takeaway: Assess, protect, apply for 15–20 minutes, reassess, document.
questions.hintContent: Recall the time limit for cold application and why a barrier is used.
questions.hintStrategy: Nursing procedures follow assess, prepare, implement, evaluate, and document. Choose the step that must come before the others.
optionRationales: A barrier prevents cold injury, but it is used after the nurse has assessed the skin and circulation.
Elevation reduces swelling and is part of the plan, but a baseline assessment comes first.
Correct. A baseline assessment of skin, sensation, and circulation identifies contraindications such as impaired sensation and lets the nurse detect injury later.
Limiting application to 15–20 minutes prevents tissue damage, but the nurse assesses before applying cold.

questions.stem: A client with bacterial pneumonia develops a fever and chest discomfort and asks how ibuprofen will help. Which explanation by the nurse is accurate?
options: It blocks prostaglandins, which cause vasodilation, pain, and fever
It kills the bacteria that injured the lung tissue and started the process
It stops mast cells from releasing histamine and heparin
It blocks leukotrienes, which cause the fever and pain
questions.rationale: Injury from microorganisms triggers mast cells and macrophages to release mediators. Prostaglandins cause vasodilation, pain, and fever. Anti-inflammatory drugs such as NSAIDs work by blocking prostaglandins, which is why they lower fever and relieve pain.
questions.takeaway: Injury → mediators released → prostaglandins → vasodilation, pain, fever; NSAIDs block prostaglandins.
questions.hintContent: Recall which cells release inflammatory mediators and which mediator causes fever and pain.
questions.hintStrategy: Identify which mediator causes fever and pain, then choose the option that describes a drug action on that mediator.
optionRationales: Correct. Bacterial injury triggers mast cells and macrophages to release mediators, and prostaglandins produced at the site cause vasodilation, pain, and fever. Ibuprofen blocks prostaglandins.
Ibuprofen has no antibacterial action. Antibiotics treat the infection.
Histamine and heparin increase blood flow and prevent clotting. Ibuprofen does not block their release.
Leukotrienes attract neutrophils and macrophages. Prostaglandins cause fever and pain.

questions.ref: Module 10 · Inflammation · What Inflammation Is (and Isn't)
questions.clientNeed: Safe and Effective Care Environment: Management of Care
questions.stem: The nurse receives handoff on four clients with inflammatory conditions. Which client should the nurse assess first?
options: A client with leg cellulitis who has a new red streak up the thigh and HR 112/min
A client who just received IV penicillin and reports throat tightness and a hoarse voice
A client with rheumatoid arthritis with 90 minutes of morning stiffness who asks for a scheduled medication
A client with a sprained ankle who asks for a fresh ice pack
questions.rationale: Airway comes first: throat tightness and hoarseness right after IV penicillin suggest anaphylaxis with airway swelling. Next is the client with signs of spreading infection and a systemic response (new red streak, HR above 90). The RA client's stiffness is an expected chronic finding with a routine medication request, and the sprain client's request is a comfort measure.
questions.takeaway: Airway, then systemic spread, then chronic/expected, then comfort.
questions.hintContent: Recall which findings mean the airway is threatened and which signal that local inflammation is spreading.
questions.hintStrategy: Use ABCs first, then acute and unstable before chronic and stable.
optionRationales: Spreading infection with a systemic response is urgent and should be seen next, but it does not threaten the airway.
Correct. Throat tightness and hoarseness right after IV penicillin suggest anaphylaxis with airway swelling. Airway comes first.
Prolonged morning stiffness is an expected chronic finding, and the medication request is routine.
A fresh ice pack is a comfort measure that can wait or be delegated.

questions.stem: The nurse is following a client's deep leg laceration from the day of injury through healing. Which finding indicates the wound has entered the reparative phase?
optionRationales: Redness and warmth from vasodilation are part of stage 1, the vascular response.
Neutrophil adhesion is part of stage 1, the cellular response.
Serous fluid on the dressing is exudate, which is stage 2.
Correct. Beefy red, moist granulation tissue shows stage 3, repair. It later matures into a firm, pale scar.
questions.rationale: Stage 1 includes the vascular changes (vasodilation, increased permeability) and cellular events (margination, adhesion, emigration, chemotaxis, phagocytosis). Stage 2 is the production of exudate. Stage 3 is repair, by regeneration or by granulation tissue that matures into scar.
questions.takeaway: Stage 1 vessels and cells, stage 2 exudate, stage 3 granulation and scar.
questions.hintContent: Recall what happens in each of the three stages of inflammation.
questions.hintStrategy: Place each finding on the timeline of healing and choose the one that belongs to the latest stage.
options: Redness and warmth around the wound within the first hour
Neutrophils adhering to capillary walls near the wound
Thin, straw-colored fluid collecting on the dressing
Beefy red, moist tissue filling the wound bed

questions.stem: The nurse is reviewing findings for several clients. Which findings are mainly caused by histamine and heparin? Select all that apply.
optionRationales: Correct. Histamine released from mast cells increases blood flow and capillary permeability, producing a wheal within minutes.
Leukotrienes attract neutrophils and macrophages to the site.
Prostaglandins cause fever and pain.
Correct. Heparin, released with histamine, prevents clotting, so blood keeps flowing at the site.
Relief with ibuprofen points to prostaglandins, which NSAIDs block.
questions.rationale: Mediators released by mast cells and macrophages each have a characteristic effect. Histamine and heparin increase blood flow and prevent clotting, leukotrienes attract neutrophils and macrophages, and prostaglandins cause vasodilation, pain, and fever, which is why drugs that block them relieve those symptoms.
questions.takeaway: Histamine/heparin = flow and no clotting; leukotrienes = recruit WBCs; prostaglandins = pain and fever.
questions.hintContent: Recall the key mediators of inflammation and the main effect of each.
questions.hintStrategy: Match each finding to the mediator whose main effect it shows, then keep only those linked to histamine and heparin.
options: A raised, itchy wheal within minutes of a mosquito bite
Neutrophils and macrophages gather in an infected cut
Fever and body aches during influenza
Blood keeps flowing at an injured site instead of clotting
Pain and fever that are relieved by ibuprofen

questions.stem: The nurse is planning care for a 15-year-old with Crohn's disease who is below the expected height for age. Which action should the nurse include in the plan of care?
optionRationales: Skipping meals worsens the nutritional deficit that is already slowing growth.
Correct. Chronic inflammation reduces absorption and increases metabolic needs, so a high-calorie, nutrient-dense plan supports growth.
Aspirin adds GI irritation and bleeding risk in a client with an inflamed bowel.
Adolescents need a chance to talk privately about body image, school, and friendships. Asking only with the parent present limits honest answers.
questions.rationale: In children and adolescents, chronic inflammation reduces absorption and increases metabolic needs, affecting growth, weight, and strength. Care includes growth monitoring, nutrition support, and developmentally appropriate psychosocial assessment. Practices that restrict intake or add GI risk are not indicated.
questions.takeaway: In a child with chronic inflammation, watch growth and feed it.
questions.hintContent: Recall how chronic inflammation affects growth and nutrition in children and what adolescents need developmentally.
questions.hintStrategy: Ask whether each action helps or harms growth, nutrition, or development.
options: Encourage skipping meals on school days to reduce diarrhea
Refer to a dietitian for a high-calorie meal plan
Recommend aspirin for joint pain during flares
Discuss body image and school only with the parent present

questions.clientNeed: Physiological Integrity: Basic Care and Comfort
questions.stem: A client has an acutely swollen, warm left knee after a fall 3 hours ago. There is no wound. The client asks how elevating the leg above heart level will reduce the swelling. Which explanation by the nurse is accurate?
questions.rationale: Mediators such as histamine and bradykinin increase capillary permeability, letting plasma and proteins leak into the tissue (swelling). Elevation lowers capillary hydrostatic pressure and uses gravity to promote venous and lymphatic return, reducing edema. The initial arteriolar constriction lasts only seconds before vasodilation, and scarring occurs much later in repair.
questions.takeaway: Swelling is a permeability leak; elevation lowers the pressure pushing fluid out.
questions.hintContent: Recall what mediators do to capillary walls and how gravity affects hydrostatic pressure.
questions.hintStrategy: Identify the cause of the swelling first, then choose the option that reverses that mechanism.
options: It raises arterial pressure to push fluid out of the joint
It increases blood flow to the knee to speed healing
It lowers hydrostatic pressure so leaked fluid can return
It stimulates histamine release to tighten the capillaries
optionRationales: Elevation lowers, not raises, pressure in the vessels of the leg. Higher pressure would push more fluid into the tissue.
Increased blood flow from vasodilation contributes to swelling. Elevation reduces it.
Correct. Swelling is plasma leaking through permeable capillaries. Elevation lowers capillary hydrostatic pressure and uses gravity to promote venous and lymphatic return.
Histamine increases capillary permeability and worsens swelling. It does not tighten capillaries.

questions.ref: Module 10 · Inflammation · Acute vs. Chronic Inflammation
questions.stem: A 64-year-old client with a 40 pack-year smoking history has chronic obstructive pulmonary disease (COPD), with a daily productive cough and dyspnea that has slowly worsened over 6 years. Which intervention is the nurse's priority to slow the progression of the client's chronic airway inflammation?
questions.rationale: Chronic inflammation lasts months to years and can develop from persistent exposure to an irritant without a preceding acute episode. In COPD, cigarette smoke continually activates macrophages and neutrophils in the airways, causing mucus hypersecretion, airway remodeling with fibrosis, and destruction of alveolar walls. Removing the trigger is the key to prevention: smoking cessation is the intervention shown to slow the decline in lung function. Antibiotics treat acute exacerbations, not the chronic process.
questions.takeaway: COPD is chronic inflammation from a persistent irritant; remove the trigger (smoking) to slow it.
questions.hintContent: Recall what distinguishes chronic from acute inflammation and why identifying the trigger of chronic inflammation matters for prevention.
questions.hintStrategy: Identify what keeps the chronic inflammation going, then choose the intervention that removes it.
options: Teach the client to complete a 7-day course of antibiotics
Recommend a daily NSAID to reduce airway inflammation
Restrict daily fluid intake to reduce mucus production
Support the client in quitting smoking
optionRationales: Antibiotics treat acute bacterial exacerbations. They do not stop the chronic process.
Daily NSAIDs add GI and kidney risks and do not remove the trigger of the inflammation.
Restricting fluids thickens secretions and does not slow inflammation.
Correct. The chronic inflammation in COPD is sustained by ongoing exposure to cigarette smoke. Removing the trigger is the intervention shown to slow the decline in lung function.

questions.ref: Module 10 · Inflammation · Health Promotion · Screening (Allergy Skin Testing)
questions.clientNeed: Physiological Integrity: Reduction of Risk Potential
questions.stem: A client with seasonal allergic rhinitis who takes cetirizine 10 mg daily is scheduled for allergy skin-prick testing next week. Which instruction should the nurse give?
questions.rationale: Skin testing identifies allergens so the client can avoid triggers, a key health-promotion strategy for allergies. Antihistamines block the histamine-mediated wheal and flare, so they are usually stopped for several days (commonly about 5–7 days for second-generation drugs such as cetirizine) before testing, as directed by the allergist. Because the client is deliberately exposed to allergens, a systemic reaction is possible, so epinephrine and emergency equipment must be immediately available.
questions.takeaway: Hold antihistamines before skin testing; keep epinephrine ready.
questions.hintContent: Recall which mediator produces the wheal and flare of a positive skin test and what an antihistamine does to it.
questions.hintStrategy: Recall what a positive skin test looks like and which mediator produces it, then choose the instruction that keeps the test accurate.
options: Stop the cetirizine several days before the test
Take an extra dose of cetirizine the night before the test
Take the usual cetirizine dose the morning of the test
Double the cetirizine dose for 3 days before the test
optionRationales: Correct. Antihistamines block the histamine-mediated wheal and flare, so they are usually stopped several days before testing, as directed by the allergist, to prevent false-negative results.
An extra dose would further suppress the skin response and cause false-negative results.
Taking the dose that morning would block the wheal-and-flare response and could cause false-negative results.
Higher doses would suppress the skin response. Antihistamines are not needed to prevent a reaction to the test.
